newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian metalworkers seek govt move to end dispute.
newsitem.headline: Italian metalworkers seek govt move to end dispute.

text.p: Italian engineering and metalworkers' unions on Tuesday asked the government to put forward proposals to resolve their wage dispute if management does not comes up with a fresh offer by December 21.
Luigi Angeletti, head of the Uilm union, said Labour Minister Tiziano Treu had accepted their request.

"Treu said yes, that if there was no negotiating he would put forward a proposal," Angeletti told reporters after a second round of government-sponsored talks aimed at ending the five-month-old dispute.
Contracts in the sector, which accounts for about 40 percent of total manufacturing output in Italy, expired in June and management and unions have failed to agree on new terms.

Unions have already called two eight-hour strikes and the dispute threatens to spill over into other sectors. At the heart of the quarrel lies a landmark 1993 wage accord which scrapped automatic index-linked salary increases.

Unions say the 1993 deal called for any drop in real wages during one contractual period to be made up in the subsequent two-year contract period. Management say not all the shortfall, caused by higher-than-expected inflation, need be covered.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has not yet said how it interprets the wording of the accord.
Employers and unions are also arguing over what inflation is likely to be in the next contract period, which runs from mid-1996 to mid-1998.

Management group Federmeccanica is sticking to recently revised government targets of inflation of 4.5 percent for this period, but unions say previous targets pointing to price rises of more than six percent are more realistic.
The government intervened in the dispute last week holding separate talks with both management and unions. Further talks are expected to be held on Wednesday.
Many other industrial groups are awaiting the outcome of the metalworkers' pay round before agreeing on new contracts for their own sectors.
